analysis.one_liner: Requires rotating health warnings, with a toll-free help line, in all alcoholic beverage advertising.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 49 cosponsors including 7 Republicans, was referred to committee and two subcommittees and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it an unfair trade practice under the Federal Trade Commission Act to run an alcohol ad in print or on TV, radio, or cable without one of five rotating health warnings covering pregnancy, drunk driving, drug interactions, addiction, and underage drinking. Print ads would carry a boxed warning with a government toll-free number; broadcast ads would include a spoken warning and an on-screen graphic. The Health and Human Services Department would run the help lines, and the FTC would review the warnings after two years.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to the roughly $2 billion a year the alcohol industry spends on advertising — especially young people and pregnant women — would have seen clear, rotating health warnings instead of promotion alone. The bill's findings cite 90% of high school seniors drinking, an average drinking onset age of 13, alcohol in nearly half of fatal car crashes, and 4.5 million young problem drinkers, and note that alcohol advertising is the single greatest source of alcohol "education" in the country. Polls cited in the bill found two-thirds to three-quarters of the public favored warnings in ads. [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Viewers, readers, and young people exposed to alcohol ads

how_it_helps.text: Every alcohol ad in magazines, newspapers, brochures, promotional displays, and broadcast or cable TV and radio would have to carry one of five rotating health warnings, enforceable by the FTC as an unfair or deceptive practice.

Print warnings would appear in a prominent boxed format in contrasting type, and each brand would have to rotate all five warnings equally under an FTC-approved plan, so no single message could be buried.

Print warnings would include a government toll-free number for each risk — for example, a line for pregnant women who cannot stop drinking — with the Health and Human Services Department running the lines and the FTC reporting to Congress annually on calls received.
Broadcast warnings would have to be read audibly in a length of time allowing clear understanding, with a matching graphic on television.
The FTC would have to investigate within two years, consulting the Surgeon General, whether science justified changing, adding, or removing warnings.

The bill's findings tie the mandate to a documented problem: advertising is the largest source of alcohol education for Americans, and studies link youth exposure to beer ads with later drinking expectations.

analysis.who_pays: Beer, wine, and liquor makers and importers, who would have to produce and rotate warning-compliant versions of ads across a roughly $2 billion annual advertising effort, plus the broadcasters and publishers selling that ad space, whose paid time and pages would partly go to warnings. Taxpayers would fund the HHS toll-free lines and FTC oversight. [S3]

drawbacks.text: Every alcohol advertisement in every major medium would need warning-compliant production and an FTC-approved rotation plan, with new regulations due within six months — a real compliance cost spread across producers, agencies, broadcasters, and publishers, though small relative to the $2 billion annual ad spend the bill itself cites.

On radio and TV, the spoken warning and on-screen graphic would consume part of each paid slot, meaning advertisers get less selling time for the same money; the record contains no estimate of how much ad time this would absorb.

A good-faith skeptic can argue the warnings would ride inside the very ads designed to make drinking appealing — the bill's own findings show heavy youth drinking despite years of public-health messaging — and the bill includes no evidence that warnings in ads change drinking behavior; the toll-free lines add federal administrative cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but narrow: formatting, rotation, and a few seconds of airtime across a $2 billion advertising operation, plus modest federal administrative expense. The benefit is health-risk information delivered through the channel the bill's findings identify as the main source of alcohol "education" for Americans, aimed at the groups the findings show are most at risk — children who start drinking around age 13 and pregnant women. The design is reasonable (FTC rulemaking, equal rotation, a two-year scientific review), though the bill is modest in scope: it mandates warnings but leaves ad volume and content otherwise untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittees for the rest of the two-year Congress and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy II of Massachusetts introduced the bill on March 14, 1991, joined by 14 original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Jim Kasich, Connie Morella, and Doug Bereuter.

The bill was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and on April 8, 1991, split between two subcommittees — Health and the Environment, and Transportation and Hazardous Materials.
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded after the subcommittee referrals; the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Alcoholic beverage makers and the broadcasters and publishers who sell their ads came out ahead: roughly $2 billion a year of advertising remained free of mandated health warnings, and the public never got the warnings three-quarters of respondents in polls cited by the bill said they wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Alcohol advertisers; no warnings were ever required

for.name: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy II
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and rounded up 14 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 49 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the roster included 42 Democrats and 7 Republicans.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and referred it to two subcommittees; the committee never reported it out and no vote was ever scheduled in the two-year Congress.

against.name: Alcoholic beverage industry
against.role: Beer, wine, and liquor producers and their advertising trade groups
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed legislative mandates dictating health-warning language in its advertising, favoring industry-controlled moderation messages instead.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call ever occurred, so the vote split is unknown; sponsorship was bipartisan, with 7 Republicans among the 49 cosponsors.

industries.note: The industry spends roughly $2 billion a year on U.S. advertising, and every one of those ads would have had to carry a boxed, rotating health warning with a help-line number in print and a spoken warning on air. The industry's interest in unqualified promotion runs directly against consumers' interest in risk information, which is why it fought mandated warning language.

Alcohol ads would have stayed legal and paid for, but each spot would have to include an audible warning read at a pace allowing understanding and a matching television graphic, cutting into the selling time advertisers pay for.
Print alcohol advertising would have continued, but every ad would need a prominent boxed warning in contrasting type with a toll-free number, reducing the clean promotional space publishers sell.
